title: Pairwise maximin share allocations for three agents exist up to eight goods
shortTitle: PMMS for three agents up to eight goods
oneLine: Three people can always share up to eight indivisible items under pairwise maximin share fairness; nine is the smallest number of items where it can fail.
abstract: A computer-assisted candidate proof shows that every instance with three agents, nonnegative additive valuations and at most eight indivisible goods has a complete pairwise maximin share (PMMS) allocation. With the published nine-good counterexamples, nine is the least number of goods in a three-agent counterexample. A written reduction turns a hypothetical eight-good counterexample into ten propositional formulas through a normal form; six- and seven-good existence is re-proved in the same framework and injected. Every formula is re-derived clause by clause by a separate verifier, and every refutation is a trimmed LRAT certificate accepted by two checkers. The paper also proves a sufficient condition for PMMS with 3q-1 goods involving one balanced agent, and reports hard eight-good instances that defeat natural constructions.

keyResults: Theorem 1: every three-agent instance with nonnegative additive valuations and at most eight goods has a complete PMMS allocation.
Corollary: with the nine-good counterexamples of Gölz and of Bei, Lin, Liu, Luan and Tao, the least counterexample size is nine.

Ten eight-good normal-form formulas, each with 252,930 variables, are refuted by trimmed LRAT certificates accepted by lrat-check and a standard-library Python checker; every formula is re-derived clause by clause.
Proposition 7: one q-balanced agent and a second agent c with 3v_c(P) ≤ v_c(M) for the third agent's top q−1 goods P guarantee PMMS with 3q−1 goods.

narration:
Three people want to share a few indivisible items, and each of them values the items differently. When is a division fair?

One demanding answer is called pairwise maximin share fairness. Take any two of the people. Imagine they pooled their items, and one of them split the pool into two piles, knowing she would be left with the worse pile. A division passes the test if everyone already has at least what that split could guarantee, against each of the other two.

In September twenty twenty-six, researchers showed that such a division can fail to exist. For three people, the examples used nine items. That left an obvious question: is nine the smallest number that can go wrong?

This Evidence Press candidate says yes. With eight items or fewer, a fair division in this sense always exists, provided each person's values simply add up across items.

The proof turns a hypothetical eight-item failure into ten large logical puzzles, and shows that none of them has a solution. A separate program rebuilds every rule of every puzzle from the definitions, and two separate proof checkers confirm each refutation. Smaller cases, with six and seven items, are proved again along the way.

This remains an unrefereed candidate. The checks were run by the producer, not yet by an unaffiliated team, and the argument has not been formalised in a proof assistant.

The paper, code and certificates accompany Pairwise maximin share allocations for three agents exist up to eight goods, released on the tenth of October twenty twenty-six. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional mathematical evidence.
